record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on fitting Gaussian-noise inputs, but uses a modified objective that compares training and test performance rather than the standard training objective in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on fitting random labels and on explicit regularization; those cited results are not this study's results. Its own relevant experiments use Gaussian-noise datasets and a modified objective. Values in the relevant figures are not stated numerically in the text.
record.test_reason: The study deliberately induces memorization using objectives that incorporate test-set loss and accuracy. It does not report ordinary training on random labels or unstructured inputs. Under the rule excluding deliberately induced behavior without an otherwise-arising measurement, these experiments do not test the listed versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's empirical paraphrase is substantially correct: the authors report that modified objectives can make a normally generalized dataset severely overfit, that doing so is difficult relative to generalizable training, and that adding input noise makes induced memorization easier. Their broader conclusion attributes generalization to gradient descent favoring parameter configurations stable with respect to inputs.
record.recipe_differences: The relevant experiments use custom objectives (4) and (5), which incorporate test-set performance; they do not use standard training on randomly labeled images. Experiments use CIFAR10 and scaled Gaussian-noise datasets.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with dataset type and size: adding noise makes overfitting easier; increasing dataset size makes overfitting noise easier but overfitting natural images harder. For ResNet18, the paper reports that adding a Softmax transformation makes random-data memorization slow, so Figure S1(a) omits it.

fits_no_version.finding: Under objective (4), Gaussian noise is easier to overfit than CIFAR10; adding input noise reduces required epochs. Increasing dataset size makes noise easier and natural images harder to overfit, with the same qualitative pattern in ResNet18.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: When training explicitly constrains test accuracy, the difficulty of inducing memorization depends on input structure, dataset size, and model output transformation.

record.problems: The relevant numerical outcomes are shown in figures and are not stated in the text. The experiments use a custom objective that incorporates test-set performance, and the text does not give exact epoch values or individual Gaussian-noise fractions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant results omitted. Figure 2(d) varies the target test accuracy under objective (5), but the text does not state a result specifically bearing on a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Ordinary training on completely random labels, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training-time ratio for random versus true labels and convergence as label corruption increases.
Zero training error on Gaussian inputs under ordinary training, shuffled pixels, and independently permuted pixels.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test performance across a label-corruption sweep.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting, and generalization after removing these regularizers.
Temporal ordering of learning real patterns and memorizing noisy labels.

record.verdict_notes: The ordinary-training CIFAR10 comparison does not involve random labels or unstructured inputs. Prior findings cited from Zhang and Arpit are not this study's own results. Figure images are absent from the supplied text, so exact curve values cannot be recovered.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test standard training on completely random labels, chance test error under that condition, or whether architecture and training hyperparameters remain unchanged.
The study does not compare training time for random labels with training time for true labels, or vary the fraction of corrupted labels.

The study tests Gaussian-noise datasets, but does not test shuffled pixels or independently permuted pixels. Its reported results concern the modified objective and do not establish zero training error under the standard training objective.
Noise is added to inputs in some experiments; the study does not sweep the fraction of randomly corrupted labels or report test error as label corruption rises.
The study does not experimentally test weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation on random labels, or their removal during training on true labels.
The study does not measure the order in which real and noisy labels are learned over training; its discussion cites prior work.
